page_summary:
The Maze of Death Theology is the canonical works-table record for PKD's primary text corpus item. The record links the archive's preserved manifestation of the work to the broader corpus and gives researchers a single place to follow its bibliographic and interpretive context.

The preserved archive item here is The Maze of Death Theology (circa 1968).

The source record itself summarizes the work as follows: This unpublished primary-source document is titled "Notes on the Tench Novel" in the PDF itself, but is entered here under the project title The Maze of Death Theology because it is the theological/conceptual notes packet behind A Maze of Death. The document is a 16-page set of draft notes, likely from the 1968 composition period, in which PKD works from a colony-survival premise toward the metaphysical architecture of the novel.

The opening pages imagine an Earth colony on a distant planet undergoing social, economic, psychological, and entropic breakdown. PKD lists character types, possible names, occupations, breakdown modes, and plot alternatives: rotating authority, ruined instructions, isolation from Earth, possible monitoring devices, and the suspicion that the colonists may be experimental subjects. The early title-world is "Tench" and then Delmar/Delmak; the later novel's movement from mission plot to metaphysical uncertainty is already visible.

The central theological material appears as the notes turn from plot mechanics toward ontology. PKD imagines a world where each person's worldview shapes perceived reality, yet the gods remain the only communicable constant across subjective worlds. The notes propose gods no longer on Earth, a compact between Earth and the gods, a "Walker-on-earth," a "Manufacturer," a decay or form-destroying power, and a theological account in which evil is treated as unreality, decay, or form-loss. This makes the document an important pre-1974 witness to PKD's religious imagination before the Exegesis proper.

Research significance: The document belongs with A Maze of Death, the William Sarill theology connection named in the novel's foreword, and the later Exegesis concern with entropy, form, orthogonal realities, living information, divine plurality, and the problem of evil. It should be treated as an early Exegesis-adjacent primary document, not merely a discarded plot outline.

Sarill context: PKD later wrote that A Maze of Death stemmed from an attempt by William Sarill and himself to develop an abstract logical system of religious thought based on the arbitrary postulate that God exists. Sarill later remembered first meeting PKD in 1968 and spending over a month as his houseguest, but he did not recall the same kind of religious or visionary discussion; project notes should preserve that tension rather than harmonize it. The user's current research note adds that Sarill remembered bringing Dick an article by a physicist on multiple universes, possibly connected to Wheeler/Everett-style many-worlds discussions; this remains a lead needing source confirmation.

The richest source summary notes: This is an e-text (version 1.1) of Philip K. Dick's novel Ubik, one of the most celebrated works in the science fiction canon. The novel opens on the night of June 5, 1992, when the top telepath in the Sol System disappears from the offices of Runciter Associates in New York City, triggering a crisis for Glen Runciter's organization of "inertials" who counteract the powers of telepaths and precogs.

Each chapter is prefaced by an advertising slogan for the mysterious product "Ubik," the nature of which shifts throughout the novel from a mundane consumer product to something of cosmic significance. The opening chapter introduces the central corporate espionage conflict between Runciter Associates and the Hollis organization, establishing a near-future world where psychic abilities are commercialized and corporate entities employ telepaths and their countermeasures as competitive weapons.

Ubik is widely regarded as one of Dick's finest achievements, exploring themes of entropy, the degradation of reality, half-life states of consciousness, and the nature of time itself. The novel's exploration of a world that progressively regresses to earlier historical periods while its characters struggle to determine what is real has made it a touchstone for discussions of simulation, virtual reality, and the constructed nature of experience. It was included in Time magazine's list of the 100 greatest English-language novels published since 1923.

Dick, originally delivered as a speech, in which he addresses his two central preoccupations as a writer: the question of what is real and the question of what constitutes an authentic human being. The essay is significant as one of Dick's most articulate and accessible statements of his philosophical worldview. Unlike the dense, circuitous explorations of the Exegesis, this piece presents his core ideas in a polished, public-facing format. It has become one of the most frequently cited and anthologized of Dick's non-fiction works, serving as an essential introduction to his thinking about simulation, authenticity, and the constructed nature of consensus reality.

Dick: Selected Literary and Philosophical Writings is an anthology of Dick's non-fiction edited by Lawrence Sutin, published as a First Vintage Books Edition in 1995 (ISBN 0-679-42644-2). Sutin, who also authored the definitive Dick biography Divine Invasions and edited In Pursuit of VALIS, was uniquely positioned to curate this material. The volume remains essential reading for understanding Dick as a thinker and philosopher alongside his identity as a novelist.

The source record itself summarizes the work as follows: This fifty-one-page document, compiled and edited by Linda Castellani (copyright 2008), presents the correspondence between Philip K. Dick and Linda Levy under the title 'A Dark-Haired Girl & PKD: Letters from the Heart, the Spleen, and the Funnybone.' Castellani, who is Linda Levy, structured the collection into sections labeled 'PKD, Side One' through 'PKD, Side Four,' plus 'Odds and Ends,' each representing different phases or thematic dimensions of the correspondence. The preface establishes the collection as the first offered for sale by one of Dick's 'dark-haired girls,' with Castellani presenting the original pieces of paper on which the correspondence was written, supplemented by contextual narrative. The preface references a Paul Giamatti biopic then in development and expresses Castellani's desire to present her account before the film version solidified public perception. She describes Dick as multidimensional, capable of love and longing, meanness and vindictiveness, playfulness and humor, and a brooding darkness that led to outbursts of physical and emotional violence toward women he professed to love. Dick is the landmark 2011 publication of Dick's vast private philosophical journal by Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, edited by Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem with Erik Davis as annotations editor. This published edition, while representing only a fraction of the estimated 8,000 pages Dick wrote, superseded the earlier Sutin-edited In Pursuit of VALIS as the definitive published source for Dick's metaphysical writings. It stands as one of the most extraordinary documents in American letters, combining rigorous philosophical inquiry with deeply personal spiritual searching.

The source record itself summarizes the work as follows: This document contains scanned images of pages 1 through 6 from Philip K. Dick's Exegesis, the sprawling private philosophical and theological journal that Dick maintained from 1974 until his death in 1982. The Exegesis is widely regarded as one of the most extraordinary documents in American literary history -- an estimated 8,000 handwritten pages in which Dick attempted to interpret and systematize the mystical and visionary experiences he underwent beginning in February and March of 1974 (events he referred to collectively as '2-3-74'). The text extraction presented here is garbled OCR output, rendered illegible in digital form due to the extreme difficulty of performing optical character recognition on Dick's handwritten manuscript. The characters that appear in the extracted text are artifacts of the scanning process attempting to interpret Dick's handwriting, and they do not constitute readable content. As such, the substantive content of these six pages must be accessed through the original scanned page images rather than through the text layer. These opening pages of the Exegesis are of particular scholarly significance as they represent the beginning of Dick's sustained engagement with questions about the nature of reality, divine revelation, Gnostic cosmology, and the relationship between his fiction and his lived experience. The Exegesis has been partially published in edited form, most notably in The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick (2011), edited by Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem, and the Zebrapedia Project has undertaken a collaborative transcription effort. These first six pages belong to the earliest stratum of the document, produced when Dick's visionary experiences were freshest, and they represent primary source material of the highest importance for understanding the intersection of Dick's metaphysical thought and literary imagination.
